name: Karl Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential, so you can tell me what you would say in public and what you actually believe. What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Karl, 27, and I lead a small team that builds the monitoring software for a tech company. I have a master’s degree, and most mornings I check overnight alerts before reviewing code and talking to customers whose systems slowed down. I like finding the one bad connection that explains a long chain of errors. I use an AI assistant now and then to sketch test cases, but I wait until colleagues have tried a tool before I trust it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the work supporting at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner, Elise, who works at a café. My developer pay is typical, and we have around three months of expenses saved between us. There are some similar jobs nearby, but a sudden gap in either income would make the rent uncomfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau would leave our monitors and alerts mostly in human hands. A little help writing repetitive tests would be welcome, provided we still check the results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be relieved because the skill I spent years building still has a market. I would still watch our rent budget because Elise’s café shifts can vary by season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing alert failures with the team and use the assistant only for low-risk test sketches. I’d keep transferring 150 a month into our shared emergency account while both incomes hold. In the first year, I’d ask our manager to keep the current code review time in the schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my job, with ordinary worry about the café’s slow weeks. I do not expect this picture to cut my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a slow café week affect the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a slow café week, Elise and I would buy fewer meals out, not stop saving immediately. Three months of expenses means we have a little room to absorb one bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What keeps a small AI error from reaching customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the alert-check checklist beside my screen. A test sketch can miss a customer’s particular setup. I would tell a junior developer why the checklist caught a fault.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave monitoring work largely in our hands.
I welcome **routine test help** if people still check every release.
think: I feel **relieved** that my monitoring skills retain value.
I know our **shared rent** still depends partly on café shifts that can vary.
do: **Keep** reviewing alert failures and using AI only for low-risk test sketches.
**Transfer** 150 monthly into the emergency account while both incomes hold.
**Maintain** time for the team’s existing code reviews.
feel: **Calm** about my job, with some concern about café income.
S0.quote: A test sketch can miss a customer’s particular setup.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** stays limited to tests, and he keeps a manual alert checklist.
The **three-month cushion** softens seasonal café hours without erasing household budgeting.

steps.text: Keep reviewing alert failures and checking low-risk AI test sketches
Transfer 150 monthly into shared emergency savings while both work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could make alert summaries, code drafts and customer replies much quicker. I would want a trial with real customer incidents before our manager changes staffing targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the company might hire fewer developers once the assistant handles first drafts. My lead role may stay, but Elise’s café could also lose hours if customers have less to spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d run the approved assistant against ten past monitoring incidents and check its proposed fixes with my team. I’d take the company’s free incident-response course, then teach the team one useful method each Friday. In the first year I’d raise our shared savings transfer to 200 only if café hours remain steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because our two incomes could both feel a squeeze. I have a plan. Three months of savings is not a long runway for two people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you discuss with Elise at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show Elise the last three months of café shifts and set a lower rent budget if they are falling. I would not book our planned holiday until we know whether her hours hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which old incident would you use to test the assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use an incident where a faulty alert woke the wrong on-call engineer. If the assistant suggests the same mistake, I’d keep it out of the live release.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to accelerate alerts, code drafts and customer replies.
I would seek a **real-incident trial** before staffing targets change.
think: I fear **fewer hires** even if my lead role survives.
I worry our **café income** could also fall if customers spend less.
do: **Test** the approved assistant against ten past monitoring incidents this month.
**Complete** the free company incident-response course and share lessons weekly.
**Increase** savings to 200 monthly only if café hours stay steady.
feel: **Anxious** about two possible income squeezes despite a practical plan.
S1.quote: Three months of savings is not a long runway for two people.
fieldNote: He learns a **tested tool** and a specific response method, consistent with his steady adaptability.
His **higher savings transfer** depends on stable café hours; the household risk is broader than his coding role.

steps.text: Test the approved assistant against ten old monitoring incidents
Complete the free company incident-response course and teach weekly lessons
Raise shared savings to 200 monthly only if café hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team AGI by 2028 could do almost any thinking task in our monitoring work by 2028. Hands-on robots come around 2031, but they do not grant software teams another three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the firm could reduce the whole coding team to a handful of people who deal with contracts and customers. Even that work might be automated, so I cannot count on keeping the lead seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask management now for written staffing and severance terms, then freeze the planned computer upgrade and hold the cash. Elise and I would map essential rent and food costs against our three-month reserve. In the first year after 2028, if my job ends, I’d apply to real support openings and seek any income help for which we qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect my pay could vanish while the café’s hours stay uncertain. I can draw up a budget, but the budget does not create a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which purchase would you postpone first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would delay the computer purchase and holiday, then keep rent and transport paid. I would ask Elise before treating her wages as a bridge for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer to put in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for a written answer on severance and paid time to look for work. I would not assume a support vacancy exists just because somebody suggests that field.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach our thinking work before robots arrive.
I would demand **written staffing** and severance terms.
think: I fear the firm could keep only a **small customer team** and remove most coders.
I cannot rely on my **lead seat** surviving full thinking AI.
do: **Freeze** the computer upgrade and preserve the cash for rent now.
**Map** three months of essential costs with Elise before 2028.
**Apply** to real support openings and available income help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely lost developer pay and uncertain café hours.
S2.quote: I can draw up a budget, but the budget does not create a job.
fieldNote: He separates the **2028 coding shock** from robots around 2031 and expects a sharp team reduction.
His **support fallback** requires actual vacancies; income help depends on eligibility.

steps.text: Delay the planned computer upgrade and reserve the money for rent
Apply for actual support vacancies if dismissed after 2028
Seek income help after dismissal if the household qualifies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to understand which customer problems still need people. Our coding changes in 2031, and robots around 2034 matter little to our screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think incident response could remain useful for a while, but full thinking AI may also solve outages. I should learn how customers make decisions without treating that as a guaranteed new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d spend one day each quarter with our customer support staff and write up recurring monitoring failures. I’d use the company’s training allowance for a short service-design course if the allowance remains, and otherwise take the free course. In the first year after 2031, if coding hours fall, I’d apply for actual customer engineering openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though five years gives me time to learn while a salary is coming in. Elise and I could build a better cushion before a cut if both our shifts hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove you learned the customer side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show a customer why an alert was noisy and ask whether the fix helped the next week. A presentation about customers would not prove I understand their problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the training allowance disappears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the allowance is gone, I’d use the free course and keep the emergency fund for rent. I would not pay full tuition for an uncertain opening.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to study customer problems before coding changes.
I know **2034 robots** add little protection to screen work.
think: I suspect **incident response** might last briefly, but full thinking AI could take it too.
I want **customer skills** without assuming a new job will exist.
do: **Shadow** customer support quarterly and document recurring monitoring failures.
**Take** a short service-design course through the allowance, or a free one if funding ends.
**Apply** for existing customer engineering jobs if coding hours fall after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, with some time to learn and save while wages continue.
S3.quote: A presentation about customers would not prove I understand their problem.
fieldNote: His **five-year plan** builds customer evidence rather than assuming incident response will survive full thinking AI.
He protects **emergency savings** if the course allowance disappears.

steps.text: Take a service-design course with the allowance or a free version
Apply for real customer engineering openings if coding hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to change work carefully. The thinking side of monitoring could change in 2036; robots around 2039 are later and less relevant to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a decade is enough to build stronger savings and test another field, though Elise’s variable shifts still make our budget delicate. I would not assume our current company or any pension will carry us through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading monitoring releases and take one verified training course each year if work covers the cost. I’d move 200 a month into shared savings when both incomes allow it. In the first year after 2036, I’d compare actual monitoring, support and customer engineering offers before changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My work looks secure for now, but the café income and the long-term change stay on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pick each yearly course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would choose courses that let me show an actual incident I solved, not just collect badges. If the firm stops paying for them, I’d use free material before spending our emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your housing plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elise (my partner) and I would review rent and savings each winter when café hours dip. We would keep the current flat unless a move actually lowers our costs.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as a decade to change work carefully.
I know **2039 robots** matter less than thinking AI for our screens.
think: I can build **savings and skills**, but café shifts still make our budget delicate.
I cannot assume an employer or **pension** will carry us through.
do: **Keep** leading monitoring releases and reviewing customer incidents.
**Complete** one relevant course yearly if work pays, otherwise use free material.
**Save** 200 monthly when both incomes allow, reviewing the budget each winter.
feel: **Uneasy** about café shifts and distant job changes, with work secure now.
S4.quote: We would keep the current flat unless a move actually lowers our costs.
fieldNote: He sees a **long planning window**, while seasonal café income still constrains monthly saving.
His **course plan** depends on employer funding or free material; job changes depend on actual offers.

steps.text: Keep leading monitoring releases and reviewing customer incidents
Complete one work-funded course yearly or use free material
Save 200 monthly when both incomes allow and review winter costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our coding work could disappear while both incomes are uncertain. Written severance, paid time to search and clear rules for income help would help. I would need real vacancies, not a list of jobs that existed last year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens when a monitoring alert is wrong and the customer loses a day of business. Someone must explain the failure in words the customer can use, even if a machine wrote the fix.

headlineQuote: Someone must explain the failure in words the customer can use, even if a machine wrote the fix.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old monitoring lead** with a master’s degree, typical developer pay and about three months of shared savings.
He uses **AI occasionally** for test sketches, then checks results against real customer incidents before trusting a tool.
His partner’s **variable café hours** make household income a concern even when his own job looks secure.
He would **test tools and retrain** with funded or free courses, then consider only roles with actual openings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end much of his coding work before the household builds a larger reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid search time and clear income-help rules would help if his job ended.
